📖 Core Definitions

Essential Terminology & Concepts

Missing Data Core Definition

Missing Data the absence of a value for a variable in a dataset, commonly represented as NaN (Not a Number) or None in Pandas, which must be addressed before analytical algorithms can be applied.

What Is Data Cleaning? Key Concept

When we talk about data cleaning, we are referring to the process of detecting and correcting or removing corrupt, inaccurate, duplicate, or irrelevant records from a dataset.

Filtering Out Missing Data Key Concept

Once we have identified the missing values, we face a decision: do we remove the incomplete records or attempt to fill them?

Filling In Missing Data Key Concept

In our previous discussions, we explored how to identify and remove incomplete records.

Data Transformation Key Concept

By now, you have probably realized that raw data is rarely "ready-to-use." After we do basic cleaning (like handling blank spaces), we enter the phase of data transformation.

📌 Key Takeaways

Section-by-Section Study Breakdown

2.2 Fundamentals of Data Cleaning and Preparation

  • Data cleaning and preparation is the essential first step in the data science lifecycle.
  • At this stage, we focus on getting your raw data ready for analysis by identifying and addressing quality issues such as errors, missing values, duplicates, and inconsistencies.
  • In this section, we will first clarify what we mean by data cleaning (2.3.1), and then we will distinguish it from the related but separate step of data transformation (2.3.2).
  • As you read, you may find it helpful to think about how you would apply each idea to a dataset you have worked with.

2.2.1 What is Data Cleaning?

  • When we talk about data cleaning, we are referring to the process of detecting and correcting or removing corrupt, inaccurate, duplicate, or irrelevant records from a dataset.
  • The purpose of this process is to improve data quality so that your dataset is truly ready for analysis.
  • For example, you may decide to standardise values like “N/A” and “Not Applicable” into a single category so that your analysis is consistent.
  • 29 Introduction to Data Wrangling • Filling in missing values: In this step, you deal with gaps in the data where information is missing, perhaps because of incomplete data collection or system problems.

2.2.2 Data Cleaning vs. Data Transformation

  • If you are new to data science, you may be tempted to treat data cleaning and data transformation as the same thing.
  • However, it is crucial that we maintain their conceptual separation, because they occur in sequence and serve different purposes in the data preparation workflow.
  • The goal of data cleaning is to correct errors in the raw data.
  • In this phase, you work on enforcing integrity and consistency by dealing with typos, missing values, duplicates, and other quality issues.

2.3 Handling Missing Data (Imputation and Deletion)

  • AND DELETION) Missing data refers to the absence of a value for a variable in a dataset, commonly represented as NaN (Not a Number) or None in Pandas, which must be addressed before analytical algorithms can be applied.
  • This critical section is divided into three key steps for managing these gaps: 1.
  • Identifying the missing values and classifying their underlying nature (2.4.1), 2.
  • Filtering out incomplete rows or columns using deletion methods (2.4.2), and 3.

2.3.1 Identifying and Understanding Missing Data

  • The approach we take to handle missing data must be guided by why the data is missing.
  • Understanding this mechanism is vital, as ignoring it can introduce significant bias into our analysis.
  • Missing Data Samples and Reasons Let us discuss the missing data issues with the help of an example.
  • Emergency Department Triage Log Let us look at how emergency care settings frequently have missing data.

2.3.2 Filtering Out Missing Data

  • Once we have identified the missing values, we face a decision: do we remove the incomplete records or attempt to fill them?
  • Filtering, or dropping data, is often the safest route when the amount of missingness is small or when the missing data occurs in a critical variable that cannot be reliably estimated.
  • The dropna() method is your primary tool for this.
  • By default, df.dropna() will remove any row that contains even a single NaN value.

2.3.3 Filling in Missing Data

  • In our previous discussions, we explored how to identify and remove incomplete records.
  • However, as a data scientist, you will often find that simply deleting data is too "expensive" in terms of information loss.
  • Let us try to understand how we can keep our datasets robust without throwing away valuable observations.
  • We have seen that deletion is easy, but it can destroy your model if you are not careful.

2.4 Data Transformation

  • By now, you have probably realized that raw data is rarely "ready-to-use." After we do basic cleaning (like handling blank spaces), we enter the phase of data transformation.
  • Think of data transformation as the process of polishing and reshaping our clean data so that it is in the absolute best format for analysis.
  • It is the bridge between raw, chaotic data and high-performing machine learning models.
  • Finding and Removing Duplicate Records Have you ever accidentally saved a contact twice in your phone?
